content: The modified incinerators were evaluated to assess their performance, usability, and acceptability. Their performance was validated against target burn temperatures based on the De Montfort model. Users of the prototype incinerators expressed high satisfaction and confidence in their ability to operate and maintain the equipment. This data was instrumental in developing a national standard for designing incinerators used in rural primary healthcare centers. Locally adapted incinerators were successfully constructed in remote areas of Sierra Leone using local labor and materials. After 12 months of regular use, the prototype incinerators continued to function effectively and were monitored by the Ministry of Health and Sanitation (MOHS). Recognizing the critical role of healthcare waste technicians in maintaining these systems, new technical and operational manuals were integrated into training packages for healthcare waste workers. However, challenges persist. Operators of waste treatment systems remain an underappreciated workforce, which threatens the scalability and sustainability of these efforts. Additionally, understaffing and high turnover rates in small health posts contribute to gaps in knowledge regarding infection prevention and control (IPC) processes and effective waste management. Proper waste segregation is essential to minimize the volume of waste requiring treatment and to recycle non-infectious waste. Investments are needed to support the construction and sustained operation of appropriate waste treatment systems that reduce health and environmental risks in low-resource settings. In Nepal, bio-digesters were introduced to manage infectious organic waste, such as food waste from patient kitchens and canteens, and placental waste from maternity departments. These wastes, if not managed properly, attract disease vectors and can contaminate the environment. In 2011, Bir Hospital in Kathmandu installed a bio-digester for food waste management. Subsequently, Nepalese engineers designed a gravity-driven bio-digester based on WHO recommendations. The system includes separate chambers for placental and food waste, seeded with cow dung to provide methanogenic bacteria, ensuring a healthy bacterial community. The slurry is diverted to the sewer to mitigate risks from further handling. Regular monitoring helps identify and resolve issues. These bio-digesters treat up to 220 kg of waste per day, with biogas used in facility kitchens. The model has been replicated in Tanzania and is planned for Madagascar. In Madagascar, the government applied a three-star competitive rating program to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare facilities. Starting in 2014, the program expanded to 10 of 22 regions, equipping facilities with ceramic filters for safe drinking water, handwashing stations, and soap. Health personnel received training and incentives to promote hygiene practices and household water treatment methods. Facilities progress from one to three stars by improving infrastructure and hygiene promotion activities, aiming to meet national standards. By 2018, the program reached 590 rural healthcare facilities, representing 20% of the country's rural primary healthcare centers. Improvements in WASH have increased patient satisfaction and trust in healthcare services while promoting safer and more environmentally friendly waste destruction methods. Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) has been recommended by WHO since 2009 as a life-saving technology for hand hygiene in healthcare settings. WHO has provided a formula and implementation guide to facilitate local production of ABHR globally. In 2015, ABHR was included in the WHO List of Essential Medicines. While ABHR is effective in improving hand hygiene, it is not a substitute for safe, reliable water supplies, which are essential for various healthcare activities, including childbirth and cleaning. Efforts to secure water supplies should not be derailed by the availability of ABHR. Low-cost options, such as covered buckets with taps, can provide interim solutions for handwashing and drinking water at points of care. In Uganda, recognizing the need for reliable WASH data for planning and budgeting, the Ministry of Health incorporated WASH indicators into the national health management information system (HMIS) in 2016. These indicators are embedded in electronic health monitoring systems, such as the District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2). Standardizing indicators with global monitoring systems while retaining national context flexibility remains a challenge. However, harmonizing data allows for better analyses over time and across countries. In Lao PDR, a 2014 assessment revealed that over half of health centers and district hospitals lacked functional water and sanitation services. From 2017 to 2018, the National Centre for Environmental Health and Water Supply developed a national policy on WASH in healthcare facilities. Basic environmental health standards were established based on WHO guidance, and the WASH FIT tool was introduced in 2018 to implement the policy at the facility level. In Tanzania, the Soapbox Collaborative developed the TEACH CLEAN training package to address inadequate training and supervision of hospital cleaners. Between 2013 and 2017, needs assessments identified insufficient resources and poor infrastructure as barriers to maintaining safe and hygienic healthcare environments. In 2018, the TEACH CLEAN package was adapted by Tanzania's national training institute as part of a research study evaluating changes in cleaning behavior and hygiene levels. The findings will inform the adaptation and implementation of TEACH CLEAN in other contexts.
